gdp-ppp-per-capita.why: PPP rates are revised yearly; an old figure (Venezuela 2011) would rank among current ones.

gdp-growth.why: Growth swings by ten points a year in small economies; only this year and last are comparable.

inflation.why: Only this year and last, or a 2022 value (Sudan) would rank under a 2025 heading.

unemployment.why: ILO modelled estimates cover almost every country for the latest year, so older values only add noise.

co2-per-capita.why: EDGAR has no estimate for some small US territories and Pacific islands and reports 0 or ~0.002 t for them (Guam). It counts the Faroe Islands with Denmark (0.04 t left, ~14 t is real) and puts ~83 t on Palau (marine fuel sold there) against ~12 t in national inventories.

exports.why: The US and some others report a year late; four years keeps them, older trade values mislead.

imports.why: Same window as exports, so the two tables list the same countries.

health-spending-per-capita.why: WHO data lags about two years; most countries report the year before last.

female-labor-force.why: ILO modelled estimates cover almost every country for the latest year.

gni-per-capita.why: Atlas GNI is converted at a three-year average exchange rate that is redone every year; only this year and last are comparable.

youth-unemployment.why: ILO modelled estimates cover almost every country for the latest year.

remittances.why: Remittance flows swing with exchange rates and GDP revisions; three years keeps late reporters without old values.

foreign-reserves.why: Reserves move with gold prices and interventions every year; older figures would rank against current ones. The World Bank has no world total, so no share column.

military-spending.why: SIPRI covers almost every country for the latest year; an older figure for a country at war would mislead.

military-spending-gdp.why: Same window as military spending: SIPRI's share-of-GDP series is updated with the dollar series, so older values would rank under the newer heading.

rd-spending.why: UNESCO R&D surveys lag two to three years; most countries report the year before last or earlier.

international-migrants.why: UN DESA estimates are rounded to 0.1%; a 0 is a missing estimate (Saint-Martin, where most residents were born abroad, is listed at 0).

physicians.why: WHO workforce counts lag about two years and many countries report every few years; older counts mislead.

education-spending.why: UNESCO education spending lags one to three years. Somalia is reported at 0.00001% of GDP, a placeholder for an unmeasured budget.

co2-emissions.why: Under 0.005 Mt would show as 0.00 at the stored precision. Same skips as CO2 per capita: EDGAR reports 0 to 0.0003 Mt for small US territories and Pacific islands it has no estimate for (Guam emits over 1 Mt), counts the Faroe Islands with Denmark and puts marine fuel sold in Palau on Palau.

electricity-consumption.why: Only this year and last, so a decade-old figure does not rank with current ones.

mobile-subscriptions.why: ITU data lags a year or two for many countries; three years keeps them without old values. Fiji jumps from 112 to 574 subscriptions per 100 people in two years, a reporting artifact.

broadband-subscriptions.why: ITU data lags a year or two for many countries; three years keeps them without old values. Chad is reported as exactly 0 every year, a placeholder for 'no data'; anything under 0.005 would show as 0.00 at the stored precision, so it is left out too.

gdp-ppp.why: PPP totals are rebased to new price comparisons every year; only this year and last are comparable. Shown without a $ sign: these are international dollars, not US dollars.

gini-index.why: Gini comes from household surveys run every few years; the latest survey within ten years, so a figure from before a country's recent growth does not rank. The World Bank has no world Gini.

poverty-rate.why: Same household surveys as the Gini index, run every few years; the latest within ten years. A 0.0 is a real survey result (under 0.05% below $3.00 a day), not a placeholder, so there is no floor.

homicide-rate.why: UNODC counts lag one to three years and some countries report every few years; five years keeps them without old values. Two decimals so the safest countries (0.07 to 0.3) are not all shown as 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3.

literacy-rate.why: UNESCO literacy figures come from censuses and surveys every several years; the latest within ten years. Most high-income countries no longer measure adult literacy, so they are not in the list.

alcohol-consumption.why: WHO lists several countries at exactly 0 litres, a placeholder for a ban where unrecorded drinking is not estimated; anything under 0.005 would show as 0.00 at the stored precision. Two decimals so the lowest countries (0.01 to 0.2 litres) are not all shown as 0.0 or 0.1.
